To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
an apoplastic isoenzyme of peroxidase from zucchini is able to bind to Ca2+-pectates, which is a prerequisite for its proper positioning on cell walls.
an apoplastic isoperiodase from zucchini was shown to bind to polygalacturonate in their Ca2+ induced conformation.
the binding of the apoplastic isozyme of peroxidase to Ca2+-pectins is mediated by four arginines clustered in the protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a Ca2+–pectate binding site in an isoperoxidases from the plant extracellular matrix.
the molecular mechanisms of the interaction of plant peroxidases with pectins, a key step for the understanding of the function of these enzymes.
the molecular mechanisms of cell wall binding and the possible function of APRX in the plant apoplast.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
APRX binds Ca2+-pectates via a cluster of four arginines, and this binding is important for the proper positioning of the enzyme in cell walls.
the Ca2+-pectin binding motif of the APRX is formed by four clustered basic amino acids.
the Ca2+-pectin binding site is formed by four arginines in the vicinity of the active site of the enzyme.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ca2+-pectin binding motif is a novel feature of apoplastic plant peroxidases.
APRX is able to bind Ca2+, which is important for the enzyme’s activity, and to Ca2+-pectic structures, which is necessary for enzyme positioning.
APRX is a cell wall–bound isoperoxidases that can be activated by H2O2, which is produced by the action of cell wall-bound peroxidases on cell wall–associated H2O2-producing systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
APRX, like many other apoplastic proteins, is able to interact with pectic domains.
the binding site is not essential for the catalytic activity of APRX, but is required for its proper localization in cell walls.
the binding site for Ca2+-pectates is conserved in APRXs from different plant species and is located at a similar position in the protein structure.
